name: Letter to My Father
blurb: Reading an angry letter written at nineteen, never sent, and finding a reply on the back
title: Letter to My Father: Dramatic Monologue Script (3 Min)
description: A 3-minute dramatic monologue for 1 actor of any gender: reading aloud an angry letter never sent to a father, which turns to understanding. Free to perform.
h1: Letter to My Father: a 3-Minute Dramatic Monologue for 1 Actor
logline: Clearing out their late father's flat, Alex finds a letter they wrote at nineteen and never sent: every missed school play, every word he never said. Alex reads it aloud, still angry, until they turn the page over.
setting: A bare room in an emptied flat, night. Props: a shoebox, a folded sheet of lined paper, a chair, a pen.

roles.name: Alex
roles.note: 30 to 45, any gender. Clearing a late father's flat. Still angry at him, and tired of being angry.

script.scene: SCENE 1 – An emptied flat at night

script.action: A single chair. A shoebox on the floor. ALEX sits, lifts out a folded sheet of lined paper, and recognises the handwriting. Their own.

script.say: Oh, no. No, no. I was nineteen.
Dad. I'm writing this because you never listen when I talk, so maybe you'll read.
Strong start. I was very proud of that line.

You missed my school play. I was the lead. I looked for you in the third row the whole time, because you said third row. You missed the final, when I scored. You came to my graduation in your work clothes and you left before the photos. Everybody else's father stayed for the photos.

script.action: Alex stops. Looks up. Nods to themselves.

script.say: That's all true, by the way. I'm not taking any of it back.

You never once said you were proud of me. Not once. Mum said you were. Mum said you told the neighbours. But you never told me. And I'm done waiting. When I leave for the city, I'm not calling. You can find out how I am from the neighbours.

script.action: A long pause. Alex lowers the page.

script.say: And I didn't call. Not much. Birthdays. He'd say, all right? And I'd say, all right. And that was a whole year.
I never sent this. I left it in my old desk drawer, the day I moved out. I thought I'd thrown it away.

script.action: Alex looks at the shoebox. Realises where it came from.

script.say: This was in his wardrobe. Why was this in his wardrobe?

script.action: Alex turns the page over. There is different handwriting on the back. Alex reads, quietly at first.

script.say: You're right. About all of it. The play was on a Thursday. I did the night shift Thursdays, and the day shift at the yard, because we had the roof to fix and your school trip to pay for. I stood at the back for the second half. In my work clothes. I didn't sit in the third row because I smelled of the yard and I didn't want your friends to see.

I left before the photos because I didn't want to be in them looking like that. That was my pride, not yours. I'm sorry. I never learned how to say the word to your face. My father never said it to me. So I'm writing it here, where you won't have to hear me get it wrong. I'm proud of you. I have been since the third row.

script.action: Alex holds the page against their chest. A long silence.

script.say: Twenty years. It was in his wardrobe for twenty years. He never sent it either. We were both just waiting. Two stubborn idiots, waiting for the other one to go first.

script.action: Alex takes the pen from the box. Uses the shoebox lid as a desk. Writes, saying it aloud.

script.say: Dad. I got your letter. It took a while. The post was slow.

script.action: Alex folds both letters together, puts them back in the box, and closes the lid. Lights down.

ul: One chair, one shoebox, nothing else. The empty room tells the audience the father is gone before a word is said.
Keep the box on the floor so Alex has to reach down into the past. Lifting the letter out is the first image.
Turning the page over is the turning point of the whole piece. Do it slowly, facing the audience, so they see the second handwriting before Alex reads it.
Stand up or move only once, if at all, and save it for He stood at the back. Stillness makes the monologue feel bigger.
For a self-tape, frame a medium close-up from slightly below, with a soft lamp as the only light. For audio, rustle real paper and let the pen scratch on the last lines.
There are three voices: Alex now, Alex at nineteen in the letter, and the father on the back. Let the nineteen-year-old be hotter and faster than the adult, and the father slower and plainer.
Do not play the anger as an act. Alex still agrees with the letter, and says so. That honesty makes the turn earn its place.
The pause after Why was this in his wardrobe should be long enough for the audience to guess before Alex does.
Avoid crying through the father's letter. Try to read it steadily and let the voice break on one line only, the third row.
The last line, I'm proud of you too, is small and almost surprised. If you push it, it turns sentimental.
Make it a mother, a grandparent or an older sibling; change the shifts and the yard to any hard job, such as a market stall, a taxi or a kitchen.
Keep the father alive and in hospital: the last line becomes Alex deciding to take both letters to him in the morning.
Turn it into a duet by adding the father as a voice, reading his reply from the dark at the back of the stage.

prompts.keyframe: An emptied flat at night, bare walls, a single wooden chair, an adult sitting with an open shoebox on the floor holding a folded lined letter, one warm lamp casting long shadows, cinematic still, 16:9, quiet and melancholy.
shots: Medium close-up, static camera, an adult reads a handwritten letter aloud with rising anger in an empty room, warm lamp light, tense mood.
Close-up on hands slowly turning a sheet of lined paper over to reveal different handwriting on the back, slow push-in, hushed mood.
Medium shot, an adult writes on a sheet of paper resting on a shoebox lid, then folds two letters together and closes the box, lights fade, bittersweet.

faq.q: Is Letter to My Father good for an audition monologue?
faq.a: Yes. It runs about 3 minutes, has a clear arc from anger to understanding, and lets you show three voices in one piece. For a 2-minute slot, cut from the first reading straight to turning the page over.

faq.q: Can I perform it as a woman, or change father to mother?
faq.a: Yes. Alex can be any gender, and the parent can be changed to any relative; only the pronouns in the reply need to change.

faq.q: Can I use it in a competition or on a monetised channel?
faq.a: Yes. The monologue is original and released under CC BY 4.0. Perform it, film it or record it anywhere and credit Script: cv.cm.
